title: Citizens are increasingly open to AI-enabled government services, but legitimacy depends on visible human oversight, appeals, and public reporting
source_unit: Boston Consulting Group, 2026 Digital Government Citizen Survey
geography: 44 countries and 48,500 respondents; regional comparisons include the Americas, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East and Africa

observations.period: 2026 survey; public use and government digital-service expectations

two_year_change.unit: percentage-point increase in weekly AI use over two years

digital_service_context.value: government digital services are described as increasingly essential while usage, adoption, and quality have risen alongside falling citizen satisfaction

mandate_route.value: citizen AI use raises expectations that public services should become more capable, personalized, and responsive

observations.method: BCG biennial Digital Government Citizen Survey across 44 countries, using self-reported citizen experience and attitudes toward government digital services and AI.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not provide the full sampling frame, country-by-country weighting, service-use logs, or causal evidence that AI adoption improves satisfaction or outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Citizens with different AI proficiency, service needs, regional contexts, government digital-service exposure, and levels of comfort with generative or agentic AI.
observations.counterinterpretation: High AI use can coexist with low trust, unequal access, or poor public-service experience; adoption does not establish capability, fairness, or democratic legitimacy.

observations.period: 2026 survey; AI proficiency, optimism, and delegated action

proficient_user_comfort.unit: percent of intermediate-and-above AI users comfortable letting AI agents act on their behalf

proficiency_optimism.unit: times more optimistic about AI benefits versus risks among more proficient users than less proficient users, as summarized by BCG

human_oversight.value: nearly two-thirds still want human oversight embedded in digital services

delegation_boundary.value: comfort with agents rises with proficiency but does not remove demand for human control and escalation

observations.method: Comparative survey analysis differentiating AI proficiency, comfort with agentic action, perceived benefits and risks, and demand for human oversight.
observations.uncertainty: The public page summarizes relationships rather than publishing the full cross-tabulation; comfort is not observed delegation, and the reported sevenfold comparison is not a causal effect of proficiency.
observations.subgroup: Intermediate and advanced AI users, less-proficient users, people receiving public services, and citizens facing decisions that require explanation or appeal.
observations.counterinterpretation: Human oversight can be nominal or inaccessible; an appeal channel may exist formally without timely correction, understandable reasons, or effective remedy.

observations.period: 2026 survey; regional variation in AI comfort and perceived value

denominator.unit: regional comparison groups identified in the public summary

middle_east_africa.value: the Middle East and Africa continued to show the greatest comfort with AI, although views shifted 9 percentage points toward neutral

americas.unit: percentage-point increase in citizens saying AI benefits outweigh risks

europe.unit: percentage points below the global average in AI comfort

regional_legitimacy.value: the same government AI service can carry different expectations depending on regional exposure, institutional trust, and perceived risk

observations.method: BCG regional comparison of citizen attitudes toward AI benefits, risks, and comfort in government digital services.
observations.uncertainty: Regional averages can hide country, class, age, education, language, access, and service-quality differences; they should not be read as cultural essences or universal preferences.
observations.subgroup: Citizens across the Americas, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East and Africa, with different digital infrastructure, public-service histories, and AI exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher stated comfort may reflect optimism, lower familiarity with harms, or greater need for public-service improvement rather than stronger safeguards or actual willingness to delegate decisions.

observations.period: 2026 survey; trust conditions for public-sector AI

concern_shift.value: citizen concerns are shifting from abstract AI ethics toward operational realities

visible_safeguards.value: trust increasingly hinges on visible safeguards such as appeals and public reporting rather than back-office assurances

service_legitimacy.value: public AI legitimacy depends on whether people can understand, contest, and escalate decisions

implementation_boundary.value: accelerating AI without accessible human review can improve speed while weakening accountability

observations.method: Synthesis of the BCG survey’s citizen-attitude findings and its public-service governance implications.
observations.uncertainty: The source identifies perceived trust levers but does not test whether appeals, reporting, or oversight actually improve trust, accuracy, equity, or remedy.
observations.subgroup: People applying for or receiving public benefits and services, public employees, administrators, digital-service designers, oversight bodies, and citizens with different capacity to contest decisions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Visible safeguards can become performative if they are under-resourced, difficult to use, or unable to change an automated outcome; institutional capacity remains a separate stage.

related_sources.claim: Official BCG public summary and survey description.
Complementary digital-trust source on access friction, authentication, data comprehension, and AI autonomy.

boundary: This record adds a public-sector AI legitimacy route across digital-service use, AI proficiency, agentic delegation, human oversight, appeals, public reporting, regional variation, and operational trust. It uses BCG’s public survey summary, not administrative service logs, representative country microdata, observed appeals, algorithmic error rates, causal implementation evidence, or proof that citizen openness equals safe or equitable deployment.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official BCG publication page reviewed for survey scope, 44-country and 48,500-respondent coverage, weekly AI use, agentic comfort, human-oversight preference, regional comparisons, and visible-safeguard claims.
